title: What is object promotion, what causes premature promotion (small survivor space, high allocation rate, large objects), and how do you diagnose and fix it (`-Xlog:gc+age`, SurvivorRatio)?
shortTitle: What is object promotion and premature promotion?

s1_definition.profdef: Object promotion, also called tenuring, is the moving of an object from the Young generation into the Old generation after it has survived enough Minor collections, normally when its age reaches the tenuring threshold. Premature promotion is when objects that are actually short-lived get pushed into the Old generation too early, before they have had a chance to die in the Young generation. It is caused by Survivor spaces being too small to hold the survivors, by a high allocation rate that triggers very frequent collections, and by objects too large to fit the Young generation. It is diagnosed with age-distribution logging such as `-Xlog:gc+age` and fixed by tuning the Survivor sizing through `SurvivorRatio`, the tenuring threshold, and overall Young-generation size.
s1_definition.analogy: Promotion is like moving a folder from the busy front counter to the permanent archive once it has proven it is needed long-term. Premature promotion is when the front counter and its holding shelves at National Bank of India are too small, so the clerk, with nowhere to put folders during a tidy, dumps still-active-but-soon-to-be-closed folders straight into the permanent archive. Now the archive fills with folders that would have been thrown away minutes later, forcing expensive full archive cleanups far too often. You diagnose it by reading the tally marks on archived folders (the age histogram) and fix it by enlarging the holding shelves so folders get a fair chance to be discarded before archiving.
s1_definition.oneliner: Promotion moves aged survivors to the Old generation; premature promotion pushes short-lived objects there too early due to small Survivor spaces, high allocation, or large objects, and you diagnose it with age logging and fix it by sizing the Young generation and Survivor spaces properly.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Object promotion, also called tenuring, is the moving of an object from the Young generation into the Old generation after it has survived enough Minor collections, normally when its age reaches the tenuring threshold. Premature promotion is when objects that are actually short-lived get pushed into the Old generation too early, before they have had a chance to die in the Young generation. It is caused by Survivor spaces being too small to hold the survivors, by a high allocation rate that triggers very frequent collections, and by objects too large to fit the Young generation. It is diagnosed with age-distribution logging such as `-Xlog:gc+age` and fixed by tuning the Survivor sizing through `SurvivorRatio`, the tenuring threshold, and overall Young-generation size.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Promotion is like moving a folder from the busy front counter to the permanent archive once it has proven it is needed long-term. Premature promotion is when the front counter and its holding shelves at National Bank of India are too small, so the clerk, with nowhere to put folders during a tidy, dumps still-active-but-soon-to-be-closed folders straight into the permanent archive. Now the archive fills with folders that would have been thrown away minutes later, forcing expensive full archive cleanups far too often. You diagnose it by reading the tally marks on archived folders (the age histogram) and fix it by enlarging the holding shelves so folders get a fair chance to be discarded before archiving.

**One line to remember:** Promotion moves aged survivors to the Old generation; premature promotion pushes short-lived objects there too early due to small Survivor spaces, high allocation, or large objects, and you diagnose it with age logging and fix it by sizing the Young generation and Survivor spaces properly.

sections.s2_technical:
Normal promotion is healthy and expected. An object is created in Eden, survives a Minor GC and is copied to a Survivor space with age one, and each subsequent Minor GC it survives raises its age. When the age reaches the tenuring threshold, which defaults to a maximum of fifteen in HotSpot, the object is promoted into the Old generation on the reasonable assumption that it is now genuinely long-lived. The Old generation is collected far less often, so it is the right home for objects that live a long time, like a shared cache or a connection pool.

Premature promotion breaks this assumption by moving objects to the Old generation while they are still, statistically, short-lived. The most common cause is Survivor spaces that are too small. During a Minor GC, surviving objects must fit into the destination Survivor space; if they do not fit, the overflow is promoted directly to the Old generation regardless of age. So undersized Survivor spaces force early promotion. A second cause is a high allocation rate: if the application churns objects so fast that Eden fills constantly, Minor GCs happen so frequently that objects age up quickly and also that Survivor spaces are under pressure, pushing more objects into the Old generation sooner. A third cause is large objects. Some collectors allocate objects above a size threshold directly into the Old generation, bypassing the Young generation entirely, because they would not fit or would dominate a Survivor space; in G1 these are Humongous objects that go straight into special Old regions.

The damage from premature promotion is indirect but serious. Objects that should have died cheaply in a Minor GC instead land in the Old generation, where they become garbage that only an expensive old-generation or Full GC can reclaim. The Old generation therefore fills faster, Full GCs happen more often, and application pauses grow. Essentially, cheap young death is converted into expensive old cleanup, which is exactly backwards from what the generational design intends.

Diagnosis starts with the age distribution. The flag `-Xlog:gc+age=trace` prints, after each Minor GC, a histogram of how many bytes of survivors exist at each age, and it shows the "desired survivor size" the collector is targeting. If you see survivors consistently overflowing or the tenuring threshold being dynamically lowered to one, that is a strong sign Survivor spaces are too small and objects are promoting early. You also watch the ratio of promoted bytes to allocated bytes and the frequency of old-generation collections. The fixes follow the diagnosis. You enlarge the Young generation so Eden and the Survivors have more room, using `-Xmn` or the newer ratios. You adjust `-XX:SurvivorRatio`, which sets the size of Eden relative to each Survivor space; a smaller ratio means proportionally larger Survivor spaces, giving survivors room to age instead of overflowing. You may set `-XX:MaxTenuringThreshold` appropriately so objects get enough collections to die young. For large-object-driven promotion you reduce needless large allocations or, in G1, tune the region and Humongous handling. A senior nuance is that in G1 you usually set a pause-time goal and let G1 size generations adaptively rather than hand-tuning SurvivorRatio, and the real fix is often in the application: stop allocating giant transient arrays, reuse buffers, and avoid churn, because no amount of flag tuning beats generating less garbage in the first place.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's statement-generation service built a large temporary byte array per statement. These arrays were short-lived but too big for the small Survivor spaces, so they were promoted straight to the Old generation, which filled quickly and triggered frequent Full GCs. This is exactly premature promotion caused by large objects and small Survivor spaces.

Problem 2 — The team needed to see the evidence before tuning blindly. This is exactly what age-distribution logging provides, because the histogram showed survivors overflowing and the tenuring threshold dropping, pointing straight at Survivor sizing.

In the mini-project we build a statement workload that allocates large short-lived buffers, read the garbage-collector beans to observe old-generation collection pressure, and log guidance on the diagnostic flags and SurvivorRatio tuning. The demo is designed to be rerun with different Young-generation and SurvivorRatio settings to show the improvement.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile the demo
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/promotion/PromotionDemo.java

# BAD: small young gen + small survivors → premature promotion, many Old GCs
java -Xms256m -Xmx256m -Xmn32m -XX:SurvivorRatio=32 \
     -Xlog:gc+age=trace:stdout \
     -cp out com.bank.promotion.PromotionDemo

# BETTER: larger young gen + larger survivors → survivors age, fewer Old GCs
java -Xms256m -Xmx256m -Xmn128m -XX:SurvivorRatio=6 \
     -Xlog:gc+age=trace:stdout \
     -cp out com.bank.promotion.PromotionDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: twenty thousand statement generations, each allocating a five-hundred-twelve-kilobyte transient buffer that becomes garbage immediately.

Step 1: At startup the reporter logs baseline young and old collection counts, typically zero.

Step 2: The loop allocates a large buffer per statement. Each buffer is used once and then dropped, so it is logically short-lived and should die in a Minor GC.

Step 3: If the Young generation and Survivor spaces are small, as in the "bad" run, these large buffers cannot fit the Survivor space when a Minor GC occurs, so they overflow and are promoted directly into the Old generation despite being short-lived. The age log shows survivors overflowing and the tenuring threshold dropping.

Step 4: The Old generation fills quickly with these prematurely promoted buffers, which are already dead, so old-generation collections fire repeatedly to clean them up. The report shows a high old-collection count and rising old pause time, the signature of premature promotion.

Step 5: In the "better" run with a larger Young generation and a smaller SurvivorRatio, the Survivor spaces are large enough to hold survivors so the buffers die in cheap Minor GCs instead, and the old-collection count stays low, confirming the fix.

```text
[INFO] [startup] young GCs=0 | OLD GCs=0 oldPause=0ms  (high OLD count = likely premature promotion)
[INFO] [after generating 20,000 large statements] young GCs=95 | OLD GCs=12 oldPause=180ms  (high OLD count = likely premature promotion)
[INFO] checksum=140000 (statements were short-lived buffers)
[INFO] Diagnose with: -Xlog:gc+age=trace  (watch survivor overflow / threshold)
[INFO] Fix: larger Young gen (-Xmn), smaller -XX:SurvivorRatio (bigger survivors),
[INFO]      and/or stop allocating giant transient buffers (reuse / stream)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Large transient buffer (512KB) born in Eden
    │ Minor GC: must fit destination Survivor space
    ├─ SMALL survivors (SurvivorRatio=32)
    │     survivor overflow → PROMOTE to Old gen (premature!)
    │        │ buffer already dead in Old gen
    │        ▼
    │     Old gen fills fast → frequent OLD/Full GCs → long pauses
    │
    └─ LARGE survivors (SurvivorRatio=6, bigger -Xmn)
          buffer fits survivor OR dies in Eden → reclaimed by cheap Minor GC
          Old gen stays healthy → few Old GCs

  Diagnose: -Xlog:gc+age=trace → age histogram
    survivors overflowing / threshold forced to 1 = premature promotion
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — Tuning Promotion for a Statement Service ═══

  ┌────────┐ batch ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ Scheduler │────→│ Statement Service     │
  └────────┘       │  large transient      │  ← size Young gen so these
                   │  buffers per stmt     │     die in Minor GC
                   │  OR stream to disk    │  ← better: avoid big buffers
                   └──────────┬───────────┘
                              ▼
                   ┌──────────────────────┐
                   │ GC metrics (Prometheus)│ promotion rate, old GC count
                   └──────────────────────┘
  Right-size generations OR reduce allocation to stop premature promotion.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Promotion & Premature Promotion ═══

  ┌─ Normal promotion ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ survive Minor GC → age++ → age==MaxTenuringThreshold   │
  │ (default 15) → promote to Old gen (truly long-lived)   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ Premature promotion causes ──────────────────────────┐
  │ 1 Survivor too small → overflow → promote regardless   │
  │ 2 High allocation rate → frequent GC, survivor pressure│
  │ 3 Large objects → bypass Young / dominate survivor     │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Diagnose:
    -Xlog:gc+age=trace  → age histogram + "desired survivor size"
    signs: survivors overflow, threshold dynamically → 1,
           high promoted-bytes/allocated-bytes ratio, many Old GCs

  Fix (ordered):
    a) reduce allocation (reuse buffers, stream) ← best
    b) larger Young gen: -Xmn
    c) larger survivors: smaller -XX:SurvivorRatio
    d) -XX:MaxTenuringThreshold so objects age enough
    e) G1: set pause goal, let it size adaptively

  State: Eden → Survivor(age1..15) → Old
    premature path: Eden/Survivor overflow → Old (too early)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Object promotion, also called tenuring, is the process of moving an object from the Young generation into the Old generation once it has survived enough Minor collections. An object is born in Eden, survives a Minor GC and is copied into a Survivor space with age one, and each further Minor GC it survives raises its age by one. When its age reaches the tenuring threshold, which defaults to a maximum of fifteen in HotSpot, it is promoted into the Old generation on the reasonable assumption that it is now genuinely long-lived. This is healthy, because the Old generation is collected far less often and is the right home for objects that really do live a long time.

Premature promotion is when objects that are actually short-lived get pushed into the Old generation too early, before they have had the chance to die cheaply in the Young generation. There are three causes I always list. The first and most common is Survivor spaces that are too small: during a Minor GC, surviving objects must fit into the destination Survivor space, and if they do not fit, the overflow is promoted straight to the Old generation regardless of its age. The second is a high allocation rate, where the application churns objects so fast that Minor GCs happen constantly, aging objects quickly and keeping the Survivor spaces under pressure. The third is large objects, which some collectors allocate directly into the Old generation because they would not fit or would dominate a Survivor space, and in G1 these are the Humongous objects that go straight into special old regions.

The damage is indirect but serious. Objects that should have died in a cheap Minor GC instead land in the Old generation, where they become garbage that only an expensive old-generation or Full GC can reclaim. So the Old generation fills faster, Full GCs happen more often, and pauses grow. In effect, premature promotion converts cheap young death into expensive old cleanup, which is exactly backwards from what the generational design intends. In my banking work this bit a statement-generation service that allocated a large temporary buffer per statement; those buffers were short-lived but too big for the small Survivor spaces, so they were promoted immediately and drove frequent Full GCs.

I diagnose it before tuning anything, because guessing wastes time. The flag dash Xlog gc plus age equals trace prints, after each Minor GC, a histogram of how many bytes of survivors exist at each age, along with the desired survivor size the collector is targeting. When I see survivors consistently overflowing or the tenuring threshold being dynamically forced down to one, that is the signature of Survivor spaces being too small. The fixes follow the evidence: enlarge the Young generation with dash Xmn so Eden and the Survivors have room, lower the SurvivorRatio so the Survivor spaces are proportionally larger and survivors can age instead of overflowing, and set a sensible MaxTenuringThreshold. The senior point I close on is that in G1 I usually set a pause-time goal and let it size generations adaptively rather than hand-tuning SurvivorRatio, and more importantly the best fix is almost always in the application itself: stop allocating giant transient arrays, reuse buffers, and stream instead, because generating less garbage beats any amount of flag tuning.

---

keyPoints: Promotion: object survives enough Minor GCs, moves from Young to Old
Premature promotion: object promoted too early — fills Old Gen, triggers Full GC
Cause: survivor space too small, tenuring threshold too low
Diagnosis: GC logs show frequent promotions + Full GCs
Fix: increase survivor ratio, raise MaxTenuringThreshold, increase Young Gen
